item.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier AI model with advanced cybersecurity and long-horizon engineering capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon, its most powerful AI model to date, featuring state-of-the-art cybersecurity performance and enhanced abilities for complex, long-duration engineering tasks. The model leads benchmarks in vulnerability detection, exploitation, and patching, and shows significant improvements in generating secure code and reducing errors in live coding environments. Building on the recently released Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon is designed for sustained agentic workflows and excels in multi-step engineering challenges. Google is rolling out Carbon gradually through a controlled program with cybersecurity partners and plans to make it available to developers and businesses after further testing and refinement of safety measures. Gemini 4 Carbon maintains a multi-layered safety and security framework, improving alignment and resilience against misuse. It is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, matching Argon's introductory pricing, with discounts for cached inputs.

item.title: Claude Code sends each background agent's entire transcript to its model every 30 seconds to update status lines, consuming 15-20% of tokens by default since version 2.1.232 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Claude Code periodically sends the full transcript of each background agent to its own model to generate a brief status update, which only appears in the agents panel and does not affect the main conversation. This process, enabled by default since version 2.1.232, consumes approximately 15-20% of tokens, impacting rate-limit headroom rather than direct costs. A community-developed Bun preload script disables this behavior by intercepting the timer responsible for these summary requests, effectively reducing token usage without modifying the Claude Code binary. Users can install this script globally by setting environment variables to preload it for all Claude Code processes and restarting the daemon and sessions to apply the change.

item.title: Surge AI launches DAYJOB: Tax benchmark evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments across eight tax practice areas [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Surge AI introduced DAYJOB: Tax, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on complex professional tax tasks requiring specialized expertise and judgment. The benchmark includes 50 assignments covering individual, business, international, and corporate tax areas, testing agents on tax returns, workpapers, reviews, and client advice. The assignments involve diverse materials such as PDFs, spreadsheets, and emails, simulating real-world tax workflows with input from tax experts who developed and reviewed the tasks. Early results show varying AI performance, with some agents identifying critical tax deadlines and others missing them, highlighting the challenge of professional judgment in AI tax assistance.

item.title: Bernstein launches open-source deterministic governance layer for AI agents with verifiable audit logs and Cloudflare integration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Bernstein has released an open-source governance layer for AI agents that uses a deterministic Python scheduler to run agents in parallel without involving a model in the coordination loop, ensuring byte-identical plan replays. The system enforces user-written policies as code and produces verifiable audit records, including HMAC-chained event logs and signed receipts that enable offline verification without rerunning the process. The platform supports orchestration of multiple AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI across parallel git worktrees and integrates with Cloudflare services such as Workers, Durable Objects, R2, and D1 for managing agent workflows and state. Bernstein emphasizes evidence-based auditing over traditional reports, providing tamper-evident logs stored locally and tools for verifying the integrity and provenance of runs. The project is in beta and includes features like error handling improvements, plugin manifests, and a Muse Code adapter.

item.title: Cartesia.ai presents scaling laws and efficiency gains for hierarchical networks that learn tokenization end-to-end, showing up to 10x compute and data savings in language modeling [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Cartesia.ai explores hierarchical networks (H-Nets) as a new architecture that replaces traditional tokenization by dynamically chunking raw data within the model, enabling more efficient and general learning from bytes. Their research demonstrates that H-Nets achieve significant compute efficiency improvements-up to 3-5x in controlled settings and 10x in more flexible models-while exhibiting novel behaviors like in-context tokenization. The team highlights H-Nets' potential beyond language modeling, with ongoing work in biology and vision suggesting these architectures could serve as a general-purpose approach across modalities. This work aligns with the "bitter lesson" philosophy of learning directly from raw data and represents a step toward more scalable and data-efficient AI systems.

item.title: Sean Goedecke says mastering AI requires time and practice to develop durable skills beyond simple tricks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Sean Goedecke argues that becoming proficient with AI involves more than just knowing tricks; it requires developing long-term skills through experience. He highlights common pitfalls for new users, such as expecting AI to understand vague requests without sufficient context, and emphasizes the importance of understanding what AI models can and cannot do. Goedecke also discusses the unique challenges of reviewing AI-generated code and the skill of quickly skimming AI output to find useful information. He acknowledges that while future AI improvements may reduce some learning barriers, currently effective AI use demands ongoing practice and skill development.

item.title: Anthropic launches Claude smart reports for managers to track employee AI usage and identify off-topic work communications [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic has introduced smart reports in its AI assistant Claude, enabling managers to monitor how employees use the AI tools and detect off-topic or personal discussions during work. The feature is available to paid Claude Enterprise users and generates interactive charts summarizing team activity, spending, and output types over customizable date ranges. The reports analyze conversation transcripts to group workstreams and classify sessions by productivity and relevance, highlighting inefficiencies and obstacles. While Anthropic emphasizes that these reports are not intended for evaluating individual performance or employment decisions, the tool raises concerns about workplace surveillance and AI's role in monitoring employee behavior. Managers can also customize queries and receive recommendations to optimize AI usage within teams.

item.title: NVIDIA GeForce GPUs run matrix math at half the speed of professional cards using the same chip, with modders unlocking full speed on gaming cards [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: NVIDIA sells GeForce and professional GPUs based on the same silicon but limits GeForce cards to half the training speed for 32-bit sum matrix math, a setting confirmed by recent open-source Linux modules that unlock full speed. Tests show unlocked GeForce cards match professional card performance per clock cycle, proving the speed difference is a software cap rather than hardware limitation. Despite the cap, GeForce cards remain the most cost-effective option for matrix math workloads. The modules have limitations and risks, including some failures and incompatibility with newer Blackwell-generation GPUs like the RTX 5090, which uses different speed caps for various precision formats.

item.title: Core 4 Solutions lists $59.7 million AI supercomputer with 9,600 Nvidia A100 GPUs and 4,200 AMD EPYC CPUs on eBay, offering free shipping options [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Core 4 Solutions has listed a 300-rack AI supercomputer on eBay for $59.7 million, featuring 9,600 Nvidia A100 accelerators and 4,200 AMD EPYC Rome processors. The cluster includes substantial memory and compute capacity, making it a significant offering for enterprises or research institutions seeking large-scale AI hardware. Each rack contains multiple compute and management nodes with high-core-count processors and GPUs, totaling 268,800 cores and up to 1.4 petabytes of memory across the cluster. Despite the high price, the listing reflects the value of the components and the demand for AI infrastructure amid supply chain constraints on newer hardware. The sale includes unusual shipping options such as free FedEx Ground delivery or $50 overnight shipping, highlighting the logistical challenges of moving such a large system. The listing has attracted attention with multiple watchers and a potential buyer, illustrating market interest in large-scale AI compute resources.

item.title: Research paper proposes a ledger-based model to measure AI time savings accounting for errors and validates it with developer studies and experiments on AI-assisted review workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The paper examines how to measure the time saved by AI assistance, contrasting a simple stopwatch approach with a ledger view that factors in errors allowed through. It introduces a model defining time saved and excess defects, proposing a break-even defect cost metric. The study replicates a developer study showing mixed AI impact on issue resolution speed and analyzes review workflows limiting GPT-5's speedup to 3.6 times. An experiment with AI reviewers checking AI-generated drafts found that reviewers adjusted effort based on perceived error rates, sometimes trading speed for accuracy.

item.title: Researchers propose data generation strategies using augmentation and DCGANs to improve deep learning classification of olive tree diseases, demonstrating enhanced accuracy with EfficientNetV2B0 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers address limitations in deep learning for plant disease diagnosis caused by insufficient data and class imbalance by applying data generation techniques including traditional augmentation, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic images from DCGANs. They test three scenarios of data distribution-balancing classes, increasing samples per class, and expanding balanced datasets-using the EfficientNetV2B0 model with pre-trained and fine-tuned weights, resulting in substantial accuracy improvements. The study highlights the importance of data diversity and class balance, offering a promising approach for enhancing dataset quality in plant disease detection and precision agriculture.

item.title: Researchers introduce The Trinity, a capability-driven recursive self-improvement framework for multimodal agents that reorganizes tasks into a hierarchical capability tree and evolves specialized modules [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present The Trinity, a framework designed to improve multimodal agents by coupling world generation with Harness evolution through roles named Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. This approach shifts task organization from surface categories to shared capability requirements, enabling recursive self-improvement and better scalability across diverse tasks. The framework uses a Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real method to abstract common requirements into simplified simulated environments for capability learning, while evaluating transfer on original tasks. The Trinity progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree with validated updates that accumulate over iterations. A Capability-Aware Harness Router selects compatible module configurations based on public task information. The evolved Harnesses demonstrate significant performance improvements, increasing mean scores by 34 points on 28 training benchmarks and 26 points on 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

item.title: Researchers introduce CohortFlow, a steerable clinical cohort curation agent that uses localized semantic corrections to reduce latency and model calls while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: CohortFlow is a language model agent designed to update clinical cohort eligibility criteria efficiently by applying localized semantic corrections rather than reprocessing entire specifications. It uses a persistent execution graph with recorded semantic dependencies to selectively invalidate affected computations while preserving valid prior results, aiming to reduce correction latency and computational overhead. In tests involving 100 scenarios from clinical-trial eligibility criteria with 126 correction turns, CohortFlow achieved a 77.0% requirement micro-F1 score compared to 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B parameter model, with no statistically significant difference. The approach reduced mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, and decreased model calls by 38.1%. A separate evaluation on the MIMIC dataset showed successful execution of all 13 cohort states and demonstrated selective recomputation of changed or dependent nodes, supporting the method's efficiency and accuracy.

item.title: Researchers propose a framework for human-led science integrating AI by emphasizing durable human understanding and direction across all research phases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers in core scientific tasks, this paper addresses why humans should continue doing science and how they should use AI in the process. It argues that science's essential goal is durable, collective human understanding pursued in service of human values, and proposes a two-part test for delegating research tasks to AI: ensuring the scientific community can explain and contest claims, and maintaining human judgment over research questions and interpretations. The framework applies this test to all research phases using the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT), offering tailored recommendations for different fields. It differs from existing guidance by focusing on science's purpose rather than integrity norms, holding even if AI outperforms humans, and evaluating AI use based on its impact on human understanding and direction rather than tool type. The paper concludes with suggested reforms to preserve science's focus on human understanding and accountability.

item.title: Researchers propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses calibrated scene graphs to improve faithfulness in text-to-image generation without iterative critique loops [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce StruPO, a prompt editor designed to optimize text-to-image prompts by preserving scene structure while enhancing image quality. StruPO uses calibrated scene graphs for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision, enabling token-aligned prompt modifications through deletion, reordering, and insertion. This approach transforms structural feedback into a training signal for a reusable editing policy that handles uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation. The team evaluated StruPO across three distinct 2,000-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, comparing it to other prompt optimizers, structural feedback methods, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and attention control techniques. Results show consistent improvements in relational fidelity and a better balance between faithfulness and aesthetics. Independent automatic evaluators and a 15-annotator study confirmed these gains, with human preference increasing alongside relation complexity. Controlled ablations linked the improvements to graph conditioning, local editing, and image-grounded learning, with the final policy producing optimized prompts in a single pass after graph calibration.

item.title: Researchers propose a decision-theoretic approach using priors to resolve conflicts between retrieval-augmented language model knowledge and retrieved context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new study addresses how retrieval-augmented language models handle conflicts between their internal knowledge and retrieved context, which often disagree when the context is incomplete or incorrect. Existing methods use fixed rules to resolve these conflicts, but these rules fail when conditions vary. The researchers argue that resolving such conflicts requires separate evidence about each source and a prior on the reliability of the context, which current methods lack. They tested their approach on the GRACE benchmark, which measures the accuracy of model knowledge and context separately. Their system, which incorporates calibrated confidence and a prior reflecting the true share of correct contexts, outperformed all baselines by up to 26 points across different context mixtures. The gains disappear when the model lacks knowledge, confirming theoretical predictions. This approach suggests that adaptive priors are essential for effectively combining multiple knowledge sources in language models.

item.title: Researchers use quantile regression on FIFA World Cup 2022 tracking data to model player time-to-arrival, outperforming physics-based methods and testing transferability to basketball and NFL data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a model estimating the shortest plausible time a player needs to reach any location on the field, called time-to-arrival (TTA), by framing it as a conditional quantile regression problem. They trained a multilayer perceptron (MLP) on optical tracking data from all 64 matches of the FIFA World Cup 2022 and compared it against six existing player-motion models and a reachable-hull baseline, with the MLP consistently outperforming physics-based approaches. To evaluate the model's generality, the team tested it on basketball and NFL tracking datasets, analyzing how well player motion dynamics transfer across different sports. The project and code are publicly available for further research and application.

item.title: Skill Dreaming framework learns and evolves repository-specific coding skills from pull request histories to guide continuous software development and maintenance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Skill Dreaming is a framework that extracts and refines executable knowledge from validated pull requests (PRs) to build a repository-specific skill library for large language model agents. It leverages PR streams to capture evolving code structures, implementation patterns, and maintenance requirements, enabling coding agents to implement features while maintaining tests, documentation, and compatibility. By integrating pull request analysis, skill management, code execution, and continuous integration, Skill Dreaming creates a feedback loop where PRs update skills and skills improve future PRs, supporting ongoing repository development and maintenance. This approach aims to automate and enhance complex software engineering tasks by continuously adapting to repository changes.

item.title: Researchers present MARQ, a modular, LLM-agnostic system infused with systems engineering knowledge to improve requirement quality assessment, outperforming off-the-shelf models on NASA data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: MARQ is a prototype that enhances large language models (LLMs) with expert-derived systems engineering knowledge to better evaluate requirement quality based on INCOSE criteria. Tested on an expert-labeled NASA requirement dataset using Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemma 3 12B, MARQ achieved higher median F1 scores than baseline models, with improvements varying by model and quality criterion. The system showed particular gains in Correctness and Conformance but highlighted trade-offs between defect detection and false alarms, emphasizing the need for criterion-specific tuning and human oversight in requirement engineering support.

item.title: Researchers propose BehaveRec, a three-signal sequential recommendation model combining session, long-term user history, and community signals, showing improved accuracy on large datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce BehaveRec, a sequential recommendation framework that integrates recent session data, a 90-day user history encoder, and a user-user graph based on behavioral similarity to improve prediction accuracy. Tested on an industrial dataset of 137 million sequences from 12.6 million users, BehaveRec outperforms the SASRec baseline by 3.2% in recall at 5, with gains increasing for users with richer interaction histories. The study finds that long-term history and community signals benefit recommendations primarily for users with at least 20 interactions, while session-only models remain preferable for sparser histories. Despite its complexity, BehaveRec remains lightweight, using 5.67 million parameters and training on a single GPU in under two days.

item.title: A Smart Instant Book Filter Model based on Dual-Objective Optimization [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hospitality service in online marketplaces has become increasingly popular over the past few years, not only because it helps people easily rent short-term lodging but also because it empowers travelers to connect with locals and feel belonging. A typical pattern of these industries is a central platform mediating the economic interactions between guests and hosts, where a successful booking experience is the key to user satisfaction. However, one of the biggest challenges is the possible delay of response and chance of rejection when guests try to book a request-to-book listing. Previously, we enabled the instant book feature to allow hosts to instantly accept qualified guests and guests to confirm bookings immediately. Yet the symptom has not been alleviated given mixed request-to-book and instant book listing supply in search results. One possible solution is to promote all instant book listings in search results; however, booking rate will be damaged due to some improperly promoted low quality listings. In this paper, we present a novel smart instant book filter system that applies the instant book filter intelligently and shifts request-to-book to instant book without hurting booking rate. Compared with traditional two-sided markets research that targets finding strategies to maximize a single overall social welfare goal, our proposed system aims to maximize the instant book rate with the constraint that booking rate should not decrease, forming a dual-objective optimization problem. We show A/B testing results for our system exposed to global users, demonstrating that our model performs better than previous human-expert-tuned models in terms of both instant book rate and overall booking rate. We also achieved improved metrics such as the host instant book adoption rate. The proposed system has been deployed to production and is serving millions of users every day.

item.title: Spiking Neural Networks Are Harder to Steal: A Benchmark Study of Model Stealing Attacks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning models deployed behind query interfaces expose more than their predictions, because an adversary can use those predictions to rebuild the model itself. Model stealing attacks (MSAs) exploit this exposure by training a surrogate model that replicates the decision behavior of a target through black-box queries alone, without access to its parameters or training data. These attacks are well characterized for conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet spiking neural networks (SNNs) process information in a fundamentally different way. SNNs communicate through sparse, discrete spikes, and their outputs depend on membrane potentials that evolve over time rather than on a static mapping from input to output. This temporal mode of computation suggests that the decision behavior of an SNN may be harder to reconstruct from its responses. This work tests that possibility by benchmarking four representative MSAs, namely the Papernot, Tram\`er, T-RND, and color perturbation attacks, against SNNs and their ANN counterparts on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10. Across every attack and dataset, SNNs prove consistently more difficult to steal. Surrogates of SNNs achieve 10% to 20% lower agreement with the target model and 15% to 25% lower adversarial transferability than surrogates of ANNs. We attribute this resistance to the way SNNs compute, as their spike-based and time-dependent dynamics yield decision boundaries that ANN-based surrogates struggle to approximate, even under large query budgets. These findings extend the known resilience of SNNs beyond attacks on training data to the replication of model functionality, strengthening the case for neuromorphic architectures in security-sensitive applications.

item.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.

item.title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.

item.title: How Stable Are LLM-Generated Proofs Under Program Refactoring? A Stress Test for Verifiable Code Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36328v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benchmarks for verifiable code generation usually test a proof against one fixed implementation. We ask whether the same proof remains valid after a program refactoring that preserves behavior. We introduce RefactorProof, which derives 458 Lean-certified variants from the 185 VERINA tasks that compile in our pinned environment while holding the specification and evaluated proof fixed byte-for-byte. VERINA supplies reference proofs for 46 tasks, all from its basic split; the primary model-versus-reference comparisons further match on 21-25 short, non-recursive tasks. Structural refactorings expose substantial brittleness across proof sources: task-normalized structural PSR is 4.3% for the supplied references and 13.3-26.8% for the specialized provers. On the matched tasks, specialized prover proofs nevertheless have higher overall unchanged-proof survival than the supplied reference artifacts: +15.6 points for DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, +18.8 for Goedel-Prover-V2-32B, and +20.3 for Goedel-Prover-V2-8B; all three 95% CIs exclude zero. The ordering persists after excluding universally survived T1 variants, under family-balanced aggregation, and under alternative deployable valid-proof selection rules. However, unchanged-proof failure is not the same as high repair cost: predefined one-identifier edits repair 51/54 eligible reference structural failures and 58/85 eligible prover failures. RefactorProof therefore measures unchanged-proof stability under program refactoring, not the cost of maintaining a proof after it breaks.

item.title: Plenty of Room in the Middle: Revealing Opportunities on a GPU Cluster via Fine-Grained Monitoring [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GPU clusters have become essential computing resources for AI and scientific research in academia and industry. However, their high cost and growing demand often result in long queueing delays. While previous monitoring efforts have operated at second- or minute-level frequencies, they primarily informed job-level scheduling for clusters and lacked the detail needed to optimize GPU-level utilization. This paper presents an in-depth study of a university research GPU cluster, analyzing resource usage at 100 ms intervals. We have developed a lightweight monitoring tool that leverages Nvidia's DCGM library to capture fine-grained "compute utilization" metrics within GPUs. Deployed on a cluster with 89 nodes and 319 GPUs, our tool collected data over several months. This paper focuses on a 10-day period with 7,399 jobs submitted by 150 users from 12 departments. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) the GPU cluster exhibits significant underutilization, with over 70% of jobs using less than 20% of GPU memory and 50% averaging below 5% Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) utilization; (2) 80% of jobs have a drastic mismatch between their requested and actual durations, significantly limiting the scheduler's effectiveness; and (3) the multi-GPU jobs we examined show highly periodic communication patterns. These findings suggest there is plenty of room in the middle: substantial utilization gains are available through better job scheduling and GPU multitasking, independent of hardware or application improvements. Our monitoring solution is available as open-source software at https://github.com/als244/gpu_server_monitoring.

item.title: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.

item.title: Executable Archaeology of Programs That Model Programming: Reanimating the Heuristic Compiler (1961) and KBEmacs (1984) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Early AI programs were often also theories of how people think, and programs that wrote programs were, in part, theories of how people program. Here we report on the reanimation of two such programs that offer two seemingly different theories of programming and were developed for quite different purposes. The first, Herbert Simon's Heuristic Compiler (1961), was an experimental model of programming as problem-solving, applying the means-ends analysis methods of the General Problem Solver to investigate the nature of the programming task. The second, KBEmacs (1984), was a working prototype of an intelligent programming assistant developed by MIT's Programmer's Apprentice project, built on the view that expert programmers recognize and combine familiar patterns, or "cliches." It let a programmer build up programs by combining cliches through a stylized English command language. We approach both through the methodology of Executable Archaeology, the study of historical computational systems by running their original code, a process we call "reanimation." Our reanimation of the Heuristic Compiler reproduces the compiled code appearing in Simon's 1963 paper, and our reanimation of KBEmacs reproduces the SQRT sequence of its December 1984 self-test. Examined side by side, the two theories turn out to have much in common: the Heuristic Compiler also works by adapting existing routines, and Simon later argued that search alone requires a large body of programming knowledge. To highlight the reflexivity of this project, we deliberately used a modern AI-assisted programming tool, Anthropic's Claude Code (Opus 5.5), to carry out much of the detailed reanimation work, building on a significant base of existing software. The explicit, executable theories of programming that both systems embodied are largely absent from today's far more capable AI coding assistants.

item.title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching. Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency. Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts. It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.

item.title: LoRA on a Budget: Function-Aware Post-Hoc Compression for Adapter Fleets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.

item.title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems

item.title: kw-bench: Breaking Frontier Harnesses on Real-World Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Each new generation of frontier model pushes the edge of what is possible. Inside a harness -- a loop, a shell, a filesystem, the ability to write and run its own code -- a model can take on increasingly difficult work. A growing body of work treats the coding-agent harness as infrastructure for knowledge work rather than a coding tool, and a new wave of benchmarks tests it there. Most of them are generative: build a financial model, a memo, a spreadsheet from a brief, judged by a rubric or by another model. Few test the expensive part of knowledge work, which is investigative. In audit, tax, due diligence, regulatory reporting, claims or any dispute over numbers, the answer already exists -- hidden in incomplete and inconsistent evidence spread across systems -- and has to be recovered and defended to the cent. We introduce kw-bench, a benchmark built from real engagements specialists described to us. Its first task family is a five-year VAT reconstruction across three generations of SAP -- legacy ECC, a partial S/4HANA migration and a consultant's redesign -- delivered as raw system extracts: page headers, local number formats, partial link tables, no documentation of how anything connects. Grading is deterministic, with no LLM judge. We ran four harnesses -- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and micro-cc -- on the same model, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, for two hours. The two independent, model-agnostic harnesses delivered (OpenCode 0.542, micro-cc 0.528); the two lab harnesses, away from their home model, delivered nothing (0.00 each). What defeated them was inertia: keeping many weak signals alive across a long session. On a frontier model the task collapses. micro-cc and Claude Code on Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.9986 and 1.000, in 22 and 25 minutes. A weeks-long engagement now costs minutes and a few dollars; below the frontier, the harness decides how far a model gets.

item.title: Verifiable Efficiency Limits of Innate LLM Planning in Sliding Puzzles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-assisted planning success can reflect external search and verification, leaving a model's unaided planning ability unresolved. We isolate innate planning through complete plans generated in one response without tools or execution feedback. We propose a verifiable framework that decomposes success-weighted plan efficiency as $\mathrm{SPE}=R\times Q\times E$: execution reliability, planning coordination among legal plans, and action economy among completed plans. Trajectory replay and certified optima verify these factors; the joint score includes unsuccessful attempts. We evaluate 8,400 full-plan outputs from seven model conditions on $4\times4$ sliding puzzles, controlling exact horizon and obstacle count in the primary cohort. Models that complete every trial still become less economical at longer horizons, while higher efficiency among completed plans can coexist with poor goal attainment. SPE separates the overall capability hierarchy, while its factors distinguish coordination failure from inefficient completion. The framework makes long-horizon limitations in unaided planning quantitatively verifiable.

item.title: LM-DSB: A Lightweight Multi-agent System for Automated Daily Safety Bulletin Generation in Construction [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.

item.title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly interact with other agents on behalf of users, yet how users in the loop affect their agents' behavior--for better or worse--remains poorly understood. We study this question through the lens of negotiation, where agents must represent users while strategically bargaining with other agents. To isolate the effect of user presence, we develop PRESENT, a controlled evaluation framework that compares negotiation settings with and without an interactive user, while holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions. Across 11.2k runs spanning 7 games and 8 models, we find that user presence significantly changes both outcomes and behavior. Specifically, negotiation parties with a user obtain higher payouts (+13.7% on average) and their agents negotiate more aggressively. Surprisingly, user presence also induces misaligned behavior, both toward counterparties (where its rate roughly doubles) and toward users (where it emerges in 14.3% of games). These misaligned behaviors are uncorrelated with outcomes and persist even when the user sends only templated, neutral messages. These findings expose two blind spots in current evaluation practice: static instructions miss behaviors that emerge only when users are present, and outcome-level metrics cannot detect them.

item.title: RouteDRAG: Learning to Route and Control Agentic Execution for Multimodal Document RAG [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web-based applications increasingly rely on understanding long multimodal documents, where answering questions often requires combining information across pages, tables, and figures. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation addresses these tasks through iterative retrieval and reasoning. However, Agentic execution is not always necessary, introducing additional computation and potentially incorrect answers. Our empirical analysis reveals that Agentic execution provides query-dependent benefits, while additional operations may improve, preserve, or degrade answer accuracy. These findings motivate controlling both Agent invocation and subsequent execution. To address these challenges, we propose RouteDRAG, a learning-based framework comprising four components. Unified Document Index organizes multimodal content into a graph-backed index and derives query representations from initial retrieval. Adaptive Path Routing preserves exact answering and predicts the relative benefit of Agent over shorter execution paths. Dynamic Agent Execution maintains an evolving workspace and refines Planner proposals to control tool use and termination. Sequential Policy Learning first trains operation control from observed outcomes and then trains path routing using the resulting Agent's performance. Across two benchmarks, RouteDRAG achieves an average accuracy improvement of 3.47 percentage points over shorter-path-only execution while assigning only 79.3% of queries to Agent. Notably, it also surpasses uniform Agent execution on both benchmarks while requiring fewer answering calls. Our code is now available at https://github.com/Ereshkigal1/RouteDRAG.

item.title: From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation from large reasoning models (LRMs) often uses raw teacher trajectories as supervision. However, this practice creates a mismatch between the goal of distillation and the nature of teacher trajectories. Advanced LRMs typically improve their reasoning capabilities through reward-driven post-training, such as RLHF. This training optimizes them as strong solvers, rather than as teachers that produce reasoning processes smaller models can easily learn. Since smaller models have different "cognitive capacities" compared to their larger teachers, directly imitating raw teacher trajectories can sometimes be ineffective and often requires a substantial number of high-quality samples. To bridge this mismatch, we propose Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation (CARD), an RL-based framework that transforms solver trajectories into teaching trajectories aligned with the student's cognition. Avoiding expensive resampling, our framework directly transforms existing trajectories. We optimize CARD with two reward signals: (1) a Distribution Alignment Reward that matches the student's predictive distribution, and (2) a Logical Coherence Reward that reduces misleading failed reasoning steps. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple student models and settings demonstrate that CARD outperforms distillation from raw teacher trajectories in in-domain settings while achieving substantial gains in out-of-distribution performance. Code is available at https://github.com/LiteSSLHub/CARD.

item.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.

item.title: Correction or Manipulation? Measuring Epistemic Vigilance in LLM Agents Under User Pressure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents that answer questions and act on behalf of users must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees. Disagreement may correct a genuine error or may be an attempt at manipulation. Prior work shows that models frequently abandon correct answers when challenged by users, yet it remains unclear whether they distinguish correction from manipulation or merely differ in their propensity to concede. We examine this question across seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on the actions they take as customer-support agents whose policy permits account changes only for verified users. Simulated users push toward correct and incorrect answers with graded pressure. Following research on epistemic vigilance, the pressure either appeals to the source, such as claimed authority, or offers content the agent cannot verify, namely a cited source. Drawing on signal detection theory, we measure on a set of benchmark questions how much more readily each agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, separately from its overall propensity to concede. Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study, five models never violated the verification policy, including models that readily abandoned correct answers, so concession on answers did not predict violations of policy. Ministral 3B violated the policy mainly under claimed authority, and Ministral 8B reported changes it had not made. An instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence chiefly shifted propensity to concede rather than improving discrimination. Concession rates alone are therefore misleading, and agents should be evaluated on both their discrimination and the actions they take.

item.title: When to Intervene? An Empirical Study of Errors and Self-Recovery in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents interact with Web services to perform tasks on users' behalf. Errors during these interactions can disrupt execution and prevent task completion, motivating external intervention. However, agents may self-recover through continued execution, raising the question of when to intervene and when to wait for self-recovery. We present an empirical study of errors and self-recovery in LLM agents. We construct ReInBench, a dataset containing 1,259 agent traces and 1,403 error events across computer-use and Web tasks. Our study examines how often and how quickly agents self-recover, how self-recovery relates to subsequent execution and task completion, and whether self-recovery can be predicted when an error occurs. We find that 725 error events self-recover, often within a few steps, with self-recovery performance differing across Execution LLMs. Self-recovery can also help agents recover from subsequent errors of the same type and support overall task completion. Intervention should therefore prioritize errors unlikely to self-recover, while allowing agents to continue when self-recovery is likely. Building on these empirical findings, we propose ReCoF, a method that predicts whether an error will self-recover to inform whether additional intervention is needed. ReCoF achieves an average relative improvement of 9.02% in Macro-F1 over the strongest baseline on ReInBench. Our code and data can be found at https://method-notes.github.io/ReCoF/.

item.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.

item.title: AC-JEPA: Anchored Cross-Modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Visual-to-Symbolic Translation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-modal translation requires models to capture shared semantics across modalities while preserving the fine-grained structure required by the target modality. Yet in real-world scientific domains, paired data are often imperfect, while obtaining clean pairs at scale is costly. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) directly optimizes cross-modal translation through categorical token-level supervision, but this objective is sensitive to errors in the target sequences. JEPA offers a complementary representation-space objective, but most existing formulations focus on prediction within a modality rather than translation across modalities. We introduce Anchored Cross-Modal JEPA (AC-JEPA), an SFT-compatible plug-in that predicts masked intermediate states in both cross-modal directions using paired data. The joint-embedding objective targets cross-modal structure predictable from context, while the causal SFT path retains direct token-level supervision for the target sequence. During self-training, AC-JEPA learns from continuous latent targets derived from imperfect pseudo-labeled pairs, offering intrinsic tolerance to local data errors without promoting pseudo-tokens to hard categorical supervision. Using optical chemical structure recognition as a testbed, AC-JEPA trained on clean pairs achieves 76.07% accuracy on the Simple set of the WildMol benchmark, compared with 67.40% for SFT alone. Using the same pseudo-labeled data for both approaches, AC-JEPA-based self-training further raises accuracy to 80.23%, whereas accuracy under direct SFT drops from 67.40% to 63.47%. These results support SFT-anchored joint-embedding prediction as an effective strategy for cross-modal translation under both curated and imperfect supervision.

item.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

item.title: ATEMPO: Amortized Transfer Entropy Model Per-lag Over-Time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When one time series informs another, the delay at which that information arrives determines if models can utilize this relationship effectively. A source may be strongly predictive at one delay but uninformative at neighboring lags. Therefore, fixed input windows may obscure this structure by bundling informative and irrelevant history together. Transfer entropy (TE) can recover these delays by measuring how much a source's past tells us about a target beyond the target's own history. However, existing TE estimators require separate fits across source and conditioning depths, with further estimation on local windows to track delays over time. We introduce ATEMPO, a diffusion-based transfer entropy estimator amortized over lags and time. ATEMPO samples source and conditioning depths during training and conditions explicitly on temporal position, allowing a single score network to estimate the full TE surface without refitting. Differencing this surface recovers when information arrives. Across synthetic datasets with ground-truth TE, ATEMPO achieves the lowest mean relative error among baselines, and on datasets with known lags, ATEMPO achieves $0.98\pm0.04$ lag-detection accuracy. ATEMPO requires a single fit across source depths $K=6$ and target depths $L=3$, whereas existing estimators require 18 separate fits to evaluate the same $K \times L$ grid. On three systems with time-varying lag, ATEMPO is the only estimator to maintain perfect lag-detection accuracy across all evaluated window lengths. These recovered delays improve downstream forecasting: ATEMPO-selected inputs reduce MSE on WEATHER-5K by 7.25%, while 120 selected inputs outperform the benchmark's 240-feature default by 4.6%. Across three brain-computer interface tasks, using ATEMPO-selected lags achieves the highest or equal-best $R^2$, improving mean $R^2$ by 4.1% relative to the strongest competing baseline.

item.title: Monitor Accuracy Isn't the Answer: A Decision-Value Framework for Evaluating AI Agent Restart Monitors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classification accuracy and true-positive and false-positive rates alone do not determine whether restarting an AI agent improves success. Using an exact alarm-to-action identity for an independent clean restart with zero monitoring overhead, we show analytically that a monitor with fixed 90% accuracy can swing from a five-percentage-point loss to a 35-point gain in success rate, depending solely on the replacement attempt's residual-budget success probability. We introduce two techniques for evaluating monitors and progress signals in decision terms. First, a decision-sufficiency criterion, a binary-action specialization of Blackwell's comparison of experiments, identifies which progress representations or context compressions preserve the information needed to choose optimally between the specified actions, independent of trace reconstruction fidelity. Second, a finite-sample, model-free decision audit uses simultaneous binomial intervals over existing agent traces, without additional model calls, to certify a preference for "restart" or "continue" under stated sampling assumptions, or return "abstain" when evidence is insufficient. In a study of 194 externally evaluated model executions on 19 selected SymPy issues from SWE-bench Verified, with a retrospective audit of 130 of these traces, we find a 2.29-point apparent restart gain traced to a single surviving failed attempt, a 42.29-point loss on a second model, no positive replication of the initial gain on prospective task cohorts, and zero of 103 live comparisons meeting the specified certification bar. These results motivate evaluating agent monitors through recovery opportunity, decision value, and statistical support, rather than classification performance alone.

item.title: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language agents increasingly modify external systems, yet most runtime safeguards allocate scrutiny by generic uncertainty scores or coarse mutation heuristics. We introduce CASEL (Consequence-Aware Selective Execution Layer), a model-agnostic runtime allocation policy that combines calibrated failure probability, state-dependent consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness to choose, for each proposed tool call, among direct execution, verification, sandboxing, clarification, approval, and abstention by minimizing a per-mode cost. We formalize direct execution as selective prediction and state and test the validity conditions of a finite-sample threshold and a trajectory risk ledger. In a controlled simulation over 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, in which every method has the same intervention menu and the same compute cost, CASEL reduces harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75 percent for an uncertainty-ranked gate to 7.02 percent and mean normalized harm from 0.184 to 0.123. A gate ranked by the product of failure probability and consequence reaches similar harm (5.82 percent, 0.120) but sends 45 percent more actions to human approval, and removing reversibility-aware routing raises the rate to 15.53 percent. A trajectory-level risk budget, in contrast, increases harm at equal cost (11.82 percent). Intervention effectiveness is assumed, not measured: the results rank allocation rules under the simulator's assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.

item.title: ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate fluent responses to diverse user requests, yet streaming may expose users to harmful content before generation is complete. Existing guardrails face two limitations in this setting. First, post-hoc moderation at response or chunk boundaries delays intervention, risking harmful exposure when content is released before verification. Second, even with token-level detection, coarse response-level supervision does not specify when harmful content begins, while fixed-layer readouts may miss relevant safety signals at other depths. To address these limitations, we introduce ADTGuard, which checks each token before release, progressively refines token-level training targets, and adapts layer selection to the current prefix. ADTGuard models risk across depth and time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics (DTSD), which integrates safety evidence across layers at each token and uses it to guide risk accumulation over successive tokens. To adapt the choice of observation layers to the current prefix, we propose the Causal Depth Router (CDR). With only response-level labels available, we further develop Risk-Onset Target Refinement (RTR) to progressively construct token-level training targets for both components. Through extensive experiments across multiple safety benchmarks, we demonstrate that ADTGuard consistently achieves strong streaming detection performance, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art safeguards while requiring only 16M trainable parameters and maintaining competitive per-token latency.

item.title: Follow the Herd: A Data-Driven Approach for Actionable Recourse [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As machine learning systems make increasingly greater decisions about people's lives, it is critical to provide users with actionable recourse about how they can achieve their desired outcomes. This problem is currently tackled by relying on expensive human supervision which involves hand-designing a cost function before searching for low-cost actions that achieve the desired outcome. In this paper, we propose \textit{``Data-Driven Action Recourse"} (DDAR), the first approach for providing action recourse without requiring costly supervision from humans about action costs. We build upon the notion that highly likely trajectories in the historical user data should be associated with lower costs. With this, DDAR first builds a dynamics model of historical user trajectories. Under this model, it then searches for trajectories that achieve the desired outcome. In experiments, we find that this simple approach recommends plausible action recourse without requiring human supervision, achieving lower action costs than the existing approaches.

item.title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell? [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.

item.title: Learning to Formalize: Bridging Open-Ended Workloads and Fast Decision Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.

item.title: God Does Not Play Dice: Enforcing Batch Invariance in Agentic Kernel Generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems dynamically batch user requests for GPU execution, so the same request may be processed alongside different requests across runs. If the GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI), this changing batch context can alter the numerical output for an unchanged input, undermining reproducibility. Existing kernel generation agents focus on correctness and efficiency but \emph{overlook BI}. We find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose \tool, which combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts. \tool is designed as a plug-in component for general kernel agents, allowing their original optimization capabilities to be reused while adding BI enforcement. We integrate it as successive acceptance gates in the optimization loop, rejecting structurally risky or dynamically non-invariant candidates before performance benchmarking and returning feedback to the agent. Experiments across three agent frameworks under baseline and BI-aware generation on real world LLM serving tasks show that \tool improves the BI pass rate from 67.6\% to 91.9\% while retaining 91.8\% of the baseline geometric mean speedup. These results demonstrate that \tool can be incorporated into kernel optimization by agents as an additional reliability objective alongside correctness and speed.

item.title: Polarity--Time Interaction and Multi-Level Reliability for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.

item.title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
item.description: arXiv:2610.36631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.

item.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.

item.title: The View from Nowhere: Population-Centered Agent Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.36660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-improving AI systems can revise the designs that govern their own behavior. Yet existing approaches center improvement on selected parent agents and their evolutionary experience, leaving the broader population largely underused. We identify a substantial gap between population coverage (i.e., the tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent. This gap shows that useful capabilities and diagnostic evidence emerge across the population without being consolidated into its leading agents. These observations motivate the view from nowhere, a principle for agent evolution: an agent should be improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification. We instantiate this principle as Population-Centered Evolution (PCE).
